Flash-MaxSim: IO-Aware Fused Kernels for Late-Interaction Scoring

Roi Pony ††thanks: Corresponding author: roi.pony@ibm.com.    Adi Raz Goldfarb    Idan Friedman    Daniel Ezer    Udi Barzelay Affiliation: IBM Research Israel
Abstract

Late-interaction retrieval (ColBERT, ColPali) scores a query against a document with the MaxSim operator: for every query token, the maximum similarity over the document tokens, summed over query tokens. The standard implementation materializes the full query-token ×\times document-token similarity tensor in GPU memory, for visual ColPali at 10​K10\mathrm{K} documents this tensor alone is 2121 GB in FP16, created only to be reduced to one score per document and discarded. It exhausts a 4040 GB GPU and bounds the achievable batch size in both inference and training. We present Flash-MaxSim, an IO-aware fused GPU kernel that computes exactly the same scores without ever materializing the tensor, by streaming query and document tiles through on-chip SRAM and folding the row-maximum reduction into the same pass. We extend the IO-aware principle through the training backward pass, an inverse-grid CSR construction that reuses the forward argmax for an atomic-free, destination-owned gradient reduction, and through INT8×\timesINT8 quantization and variable-length (padding-free) scoring. Flash-MaxSim is up to 3.9×3.9\times faster on an A100 (4.7×4.7\times on an H100) than naive PyTorch at matched precision, uses up to 16×16\times less inference memory and ∼28×\sim\!28\times less training memory, unlocks corpus and batch sizes that exhaust PyTorch entirely, preserves the exact ranking (100%100\% top-2020 agreement with an FP32 reference), and is released open-source at https://github.com/roipony/flash-maxsim.

1 Introduction

Dense single-vector retrieval encodes each query and document as one vector and scores by a dot product. Late-interaction retrieval instead keeps a set of token-level embeddings per item and scores with MaxSim:

score⁡(Q,D)=∑i=1Lqmaxj=1Ld​⟨Qi,Dj⟩,\mathrm{score}(Q,D)=\sum_{i=1}^{L_{q}}\max_{j=1}^{L_{d}}\langle Q_{i},D_{j}\rangle, (1)

with Q∈ℝLq×dQ\in\mathbb{R}^{L_{q}\times d}, D∈ℝLd×dD\in\mathbb{R}^{L_{d}\times d}. This finer-grained matching is what gives ColBERT Khattab and Zaharia (2020) and its document-image successor ColPali Faysse et al. (2025) their quality advantage, and its cost. The natural PyTorch implementation forms the [Lq,Ld][L_{q},L_{d}] similarity matrix per (query, document) pair via an einsum, then reduces it (max\max over document tokens, sum over query tokens). At scale the dominant memory cost is therefore a [B,Lq,Ld][B,L_{q},L_{d}] tensor that exists only to be reduced away.

For visual ColPali (Lq=Ld=1024L_{q}\!=\!L_{d}\!=\!1024 patch tokens, d=128d\!=\!128) over a 10​K10\mathrm{K}-document candidate set, that tensor is 104⋅10242⋅2≈2110^{4}\cdot 1024^{2}\cdot 2\approx 21 GB in FP16 (4242 GB in FP32). It out-of-memories (OOMs) a 4040 GB GPU and consumes a quarter to half of an 8080 GB one, capping batch size for reranking, for in-batch-negatives contrastive training, and for distillation. The matrix is the bottleneck, and it never needed to exist.

FlashAttention Dao et al. (2022) showed that the analogous attention matrix can be avoided by IO-aware tiling. We make the same move for MaxSim; and because MaxSim is an operator, not just an inference pass, we carry the idea through training and quantization. Our contributions:

  1. 1.

    A fused forward kernel (§4.1) that computes exact MaxSim with peak memory ≈\approx the document embeddings, the similarity tensor never forms. Up to 3.9×3.9\times over naive PyTorch on dense scoring (A100; 4.7×4.7\times on H100) and OOM-unlock at corpus scale (§5).

  2. 2.

    A fused backward kernel (§4.2): an inverse-grid CSR map, built at runtime from the saved forward argmax, that performs an atomic-free, destination-owned gradient reduction, no re-materialized matrix, FP32-accurate gradients. It unlocks contrastive batches that OOM PyTorch.

  3. 3.

    Quantized and variable-length variants (§4.3): INT8×\timesINT8 MaxSim with Spearman ρ=0.999\rho\!=\!0.999 ranking fidelity, and padding-free cu_seqlens scoring (up to 5×5\times) that removes the padding tax.

  4. 4.

    An open-source release of all kernels and variants.

2 Related Work

FlashAttention Dao et al. (2022) is the conceptual parent, IO-aware tiling that avoids materializing the attention matrix by streaming tiles through on-chip memory with an online softmax. Flash-MaxSim applies the same principle to the MaxSim operator; the reduction is a plain running max (idempotent, no rescaling), and, unlike attention kernels, we carry it through a hard-selection (argmax) backward for training. Flash-KMeans Yang et al. (2026) is the closest analog in spirit: a materialization-free assignment via online argmin plus a sort-inverse, low-contention centroid update; we target a retrieval operator and add a quantization and variable-length story. ColBERT Khattab and Zaharia (2020) and ColPali Faysse et al. (2025) define the late-interaction application this work accelerates.

3 Background and Motivation

3.1 MaxSim and the Standard GPU Implementation

A late-interaction model encodes a query as Q∈ℝLq×dQ\in\mathbb{R}^{L_{q}\times d} and a document as D∈ℝLd×dD\in\mathbb{R}^{L_{d}\times d} (token-level, ℓ2\ell_{2}-normalized, d=128d{=}128). MaxSim (Eq. 1) is computed at scale in two regimes: reranking (one query vs. BB candidate documents, output [B][B]) and, during training, in-batch-negatives scoring (NqN_{q} queries vs. BB documents, an all-pairs [Nq,B][N_{q},B] score matrix). Written directly,

⬇
S = einsum("bqd,bld->bql", Q, D)
# [B, Lq, Ld]: materialized in HBM
score = S.max(dim=2).values.sum(dim=1)

the intermediate SS of shape [B,Lq,Ld][B,L_{q},L_{d}] is written to high-bandwidth memory (HBM), read back for the max\max reduction, and discarded.

3.2 Kernel-Level Bottleneck: the Materialized Tensor

The footprint of SS is O⁡(B⋅Lq⋅Ld)O(B\cdot L_{q}\cdot L_{d}), independent of dd, and it is both the memory and the bandwidth bottleneck. The naive path moves Θ⁡(B​Lq​Ld)\Theta(BL_{q}L_{d}) bytes just for SS (one write, at least one read), versus Θ⁡(B​Ld​d)\Theta(BL_{d}d) bytes for the inputs. For ColPali (Lq=Ld=1024L_{q}{=}L_{d}{=}1024, d=128d{=}128) the SS traffic exceeds the input traffic by Lq/d≈8×L_{q}/d\approx 8\times, and the materialized SS exceeds the inputs by Lq≈1024×L_{q}\approx 1024\times.

Arithmetic intensity and the roofline.

Scoring one pair costs 2​Lq​Ld​d2L_{q}L_{d}d FLOPs. The naive path’s HBM traffic is dominated by the Lq×LdL_{q}\times L_{d} surface of SS (≈4​Lq​Ld\approx 4L_{q}L_{d} bytes in FP16: one write, two reads), so its arithmetic intensity is AInaive≈2​Lq​Ld​d/(4​Lq​Ld)=d/2≈64\mathrm{AI}_{\text{naive}}\approx 2L_{q}L_{d}d/(4L_{q}L_{d})=d/2\approx 64 FLOPs/byte at d=128d{=}128. An NVIDIA H100’s bf16 roofline ridge point is ≈295\approx 295 FLOPs/byte, so the naive operator sits four-to-five times into the memory-bound regime, the tensor cores idle while HBM moves a tensor that is immediately discarded. Flash-MaxSim removes the SS traffic entirely and crosses the ridge (§4.1).

3.3 System-Level Constraints in Real Deployments

The materialized tensor imposes hard system limits, not just slowdowns. At ColPali corpus scale the 2121 GB FP16 SS OOMs a 4040 GB GPU and consumes half of an 8080 GB one, so reranking a large candidate set is impossible without manual chunking. In training, in-batch-negatives scoring forms an all-pairs [Nq,B,Lq,Ld][N_{q},B,L_{q},L_{d}] tensor whose size is quadratic in the batch BB; with autograd also retaining its gradient, the contrastive batch size is capped far below what the model and optimizer alone would allow, at ColPali shape, B=128B{=}128 OOMs an 8080 GB GPU (§5). These caps, on corpus size at inference and batch size at training, are the real-deployment cost of materialization.

4 Methodology

4.1 Fused Forward: Materialization-Free Scoring via Online Max

The forward kernel computes Eq. 1 without ever writing SS (Figure 1). It is structurally a FlashAttention-style tile-then-reduce, with three differences that make it cheaper: (i) the in-tile reduction is a plain running maximum, not a softmax, no log-sum-exp and no rescaling, because max\max is idempotent; (ii) the output is a scalar per (query, document) pair, not a matrix; (iii) there is no value matrix VV to re-read.

The kernel launches Nq​BN_{q}B independent programs (thread blocks), one per (query, document) pair; each produces a single FP32 scalar. The similarity sub-tile StS_{t} of shape [bq,bd][\textsc{b}_{q},\textsc{b}_{d}] lives only in SRAM (the running max mm and accumulator stay in fp32 registers) and is reduced to a bq\textsc{b}_{q}-vector before the next document tile overwrites it. The full [B,Lq,Ld][B,L_{q},L_{d}] tensor is never written. Because the sum-of-maxima decomposes over query chunks, a long LqL_{q} is split into fixed chunks whose partial scores are summed, so a single compiled kernel serves all problem shapes at runtime.

Proposition 1 (Exactness).

Algorithm 2 returns exactly score⁡(Q,D)=∑i=1Lqmaxj=1Ld​⟨Qi,Dj⟩\mathrm{score}(Q,D)=\sum_{i=1}^{L_{q}}\max_{j=1}^{L_{d}}\langle Q_{i},D_{j}\rangle, identical to the dense computation up to floating-point reassociation, using Θ⁡(B​Lq)\Theta(BL_{q}) auxiliary memory in place of the Θ⁡(B​Lq​Ld)\Theta(BL_{q}L_{d}) tensor of Algorithm 1.

The running-max reduction is idempotent and associative, so partial tiles compose by a single elementwise max\max with no rescaling correction, unlike the online softmax of FlashAttention (detailed next).

4.1.1 Online-Max Recurrence

After consuming the kk-th document tile, the running max obeys m(k)=max⁡(m(k−1),rowmax⁡(S(k)))m^{(k)}=\max(m^{(k-1)},\mathrm{rowmax}(S^{(k)})) with m(0)=−∞m^{(0)}=-\infty; after all tiles, mm is the exact per-row maximum over the full LdL_{d} axis. Unlike online softmax (FlashAttention), there is no running normalizer and no rescaling factor exp⁡(m(k−1)−m(k))\exp(m^{(k-1)}{-}m^{(k)}): max\max is idempotent, so the update is a single elementwise max and the result is bitwise the offline computation. Masked document positions are set to −∞-\infty before the row reduction (not post-multiplied by a 0/10/1 mask), so padding can never be selected even when valid scores are negative.

4.1.2 IO Complexity and Roofline

Theorem 1 (IO complexity).

For NqN_{q} queries and BB documents at lengths Lq,LdL_{q},L_{d} and dimension dd, naive MaxSim (Algorithm 1) performs Θ⁡(Nq​B​Lq​Ld)\Theta(N_{q}BL_{q}L_{d}) HBM accesses (one write and at least one read of SS) and uses Θ⁡(Nq​B​Lq​Ld)\Theta(N_{q}BL_{q}L_{d}) memory. Flash-MaxSim (Algorithm 2) performs Θ⁡(Nq​B​(Lq+Ld)​d)\Theta(N_{q}B(L_{q}{+}L_{d})d) HBM accesses, reading each operand once and writing Θ⁡(Nq​B)\Theta(N_{q}B) scalars, with Θ⁡(Lq)\Theta(L_{q}) on-chip state per program. The materialized-tensor term Θ⁡(Nq​B​Lq​Ld)\Theta(N_{q}BL_{q}L_{d}) is eliminated; the HBM-traffic ratio is Lq​Ld/((Lq+Ld)​d)L_{q}L_{d}/\big((L_{q}{+}L_{d})\,d\big), i.e. Lq/2​dL_{q}/2d when Lq=LdL_{q}{=}L_{d}.

Proof sketch. Each program loads its QQ and DbD_{b} tiles once into SRAM, forms StS_{t} on chip, and folds it into the running max; SS is never written to or read from HBM, so operand traffic is Θ⁡(Nq​B​(Lq+Ld)​d)\Theta(N_{q}B(L_{q}{+}L_{d})d) and output traffic Θ⁡(Nq​B)\Theta(N_{q}B). The naive path additionally writes and reads SS, adding Θ⁡(Nq​B​Lq​Ld)\Theta(N_{q}BL_{q}L_{d}), which dominates whenever Lq​Ld≫(Lq+Ld)​dL_{q}L_{d}\gg(L_{q}{+}L_{d})d. □\square

With only the operand reads as HBM traffic, AIfused≈2​Lq​Ld​d/(2​(Lq+Ld)​d)=Lq​Ld/(Lq+Ld)≈512\mathrm{AI}_{\text{fused}}\approx 2L_{q}L_{d}d/(2(L_{q}{+}L_{d})d)=L_{q}L_{d}/(L_{q}{+}L_{d})\approx 512 FLOPs/byte at ColPali shape, above the H100 ridge. The identical matmul thus moves from memory-bound to compute-bound: it is faster not because the arithmetic is cheaper, but because it no longer waits on memory.

4.1.3 Numerical Fidelity

The accumulator is FP32 throughout. The maximum relative error against an FP32 reference is 2×10−62\times 10^{-6}, versus 4×10−34\times 10^{-3} for an FP16 batched-matrix-multiply baseline, three orders of magnitude tighter, so ranking ties are resolved at true precision rather than by FP16 noise.

4.1.4 Kernel Family

A family of forward variants shares the running-max core: single-query rerank, batched multi-query, variable-length packed (§4.3), query-reuse, split-KK, and a two-stage INT8→\toFP16 top-KK scan, selected by a runtime dispatcher on (Nq,B,Lq,Ld,d,dtype)(N_{q},B,L_{q},L_{d},d,\mathrm{dtype}).

4.2 Inverse-Grid Update: Low-Contention Gradient Aggregation

The forward kernel makes inference fit. Training gains nothing if the backward re-materializes the [Nq,B,Lq,Ld][N_{q},B,L_{q},L_{d}] tensor and OOMs at the same batch the forward unlocked. The naive alternative, an atomicAdd of each gradient into its argmax-selected destination, serializes on hot document tokens (a frequent token can be the argmax for hundreds of queries) and doubles gradient bandwidth with FP32 atomics.

4.2.1 Closed-Form Gradients

With upstream gradient gi​j=∂L/∂score⁡(i,j)g_{ij}=\partial L/\partial\,\mathrm{score}(i,j) and the forward winner t⋆​(i,j,s)=arg⁡maxt​⟨Qi,s,Dj,t⟩t^{\star}(i,j,s)=\arg\max_{t}\langle Q_{i,s},D_{j,t}\rangle, resolving the max\max (a constant index, post-forward) and applying the chain rule gives

∇Qi,s\displaystyle\nabla_{Q_{i,s}} =∑jgi​j​Dj,t⋆​(i,j,s),\displaystyle=\textstyle\sum_{j}g_{ij}\,D_{j,\,t^{\star}(i,j,s)}, (2)
∇Dj,t\displaystyle\nabla_{D_{j,t}} =∑(i,s):t⋆​(i,j,s)=tgi​jQi,s.\displaystyle=\textstyle\sum_{(i,s):\,t^{\star}(i,j,s)=t}g_{ij}\,Q_{i,s}. (3)

Eq. 2 is a gather: each query token reads exactly one DD row per document, no collisions, so ∇Q\nabla Q is embarrassingly parallel (one program per (i,s)(i,s)). Eq. 3 is a scatter: many query positions may select the same document token tt (data-dependent contention), which is why ∇D\nabla D is the hard side and the inverse-grid CSR exists.

4.2.2 Runtime Inverse-Grid Construction

The forward already saves argmax∈[0,Ld)[Nq⋅B,Lq]\mathrm{argmax}\in[0,L_{d})^{[N_{q}\cdot B,\,L_{q}]}, one index per query token. That is a source→\todestination map; the backward needs the inverse: for each destination document token (b,k)(b,k), which query positions selected it? We invert this at runtime, inside autograd, with three primitives, bincount→\tocumsum for a CSR row pointer, and a stable argsort of flattened destinations for the column indices. The CSR map costs O⁡(Nq​B​Lq)O(N_{q}BL_{q}) for the indices plus O⁡(B​Ld)O(BL_{d}) for the row pointer, far below the similarity tensor it replaces.

4.2.3 Destination-Owned Reduction

Given the CSR map, the ∇D\nabla D kernel assigns one program per output row (b,tok)(b,\mathrm{tok}); it walks that row’s source list, accumulates in an FP32 SRAM register, and writes the row once, coalesced. No two programs touch the same row, so there are no atomics. The companion ∇Q\nabla Q kernel exploits the dual asymmetry (QQ is shared across all BB documents, so each ∇Q​[i]\nabla Q[i] is written once after looping the small BB axis, no CSR needed). Each ingredient is textbook; the contribution is their combination, built at runtime from a saved argmax, inside autograd, applied to a hard-selection backward, with a dispatch heuristic that falls back to atomic scatter in the low-contention regime. Benefit. Neither the CSR build nor the two row-owned kernels (Algorithm 3) ever allocate the [Nq,B,Lq,Ld][N_{q},B,L_{q},L_{d}] similarity tensor or its gradient; peak training memory is essentially the embeddings plus the int32 argmax buffer. This is what yields the 28×28\times memory reduction and the B=128B{=}128 batch unlock of Table 5, while keeping gradients bit-faithful to the FP32 reference.

4.2.4 Generalization to Chamfer Distance

The construction applies to any forward that emits, per source, an integer index into a destination set: argmax, argmin, top-1 attention, mixture-of-experts routing, spatial argmax (MaxPool/RoIAlign), kk-NN. We instantiate it for the Chamfer distance between two point sets P∈ℝN×3P\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times 3} and Q∈ℝM×3Q\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times 3},

CD⁡(P,Q)=1N​∑pminq⁡∥p−q∥2+1M​∑qminp⁡∥q−p∥2,\mathrm{CD}(P,Q)=\tfrac{1}{N}\!\sum_{p}\min_{q}\lVert p-q\rVert^{2}+\tfrac{1}{M}\!\sum_{q}\min_{p}\lVert q-p\rVert^{2},

the standard 3D point-cloud / shape-matching loss. It has the same structure as MaxSim with two swaps: a min-reduction over the other set (still idempotent, still rescaler-free) in place of the row-max, and squared Euclidean distance in place of the inner product. The naive form materializes the identical [N,M][N,M] pairwise matrix; the fused kernel streams tiles with an online min, and the backward reuses the saved argmin (nearest-neighbour index) through the same inverse-grid CSR. Measured: gradient cosine 1.000001.00000 vs. the naive autograd, 7777 to 152×152\times speedup, and 100​K100\mathrm{K}-point clouds that OOM the naive form run comfortably. This is direct evidence that Flash-MaxSim is a reusable hard-selection-operator pattern, not a MaxSim-specific kernel.

4.3 Quantized and Variable-Length Variants

4.3.1 INT8×\timesINT8 Quantization

Per-token symmetric quantization of both QQ and DD, with dequantization fused into the kernel. This halves index storage and is 4.7×4.7\times faster than a naive dequantize-then-score path at the tested shapes (not yet a net win at full ColPali scale on A100), with near-FP32 ranking fidelity (Spearman ρ=0.999\rho=0.999 against the FP32 reference, 100%100\% top-2020 overlap on tested workloads).

4.3.2 Padding-Free Variable-Length

Real corpora have ragged document lengths; batching them into a dense tensor forces padding to a common LdmaxL_{d}^{\max}, and the naive path computes (and the mask discards) all padded positions. Flash-MaxSim’s cu_seqlens variant processes only real tokens (∑Ld\sum L_{d} work instead of B​LdmaxBL_{d}^{\max}), giving up to 5×5\times on highly ragged corpora and 1.61.6 to 3.0×3.0\times at a realistic (HotpotQA-like) length distribution.

5 Experiments

5.1 Experimental Setup

NVIDIA A100-SXM4-80GB (and an H100 80GB for the forward sweep); PyTorch 2.8, FP32 matmul precision high. CUDA-event timing with warmup, median of repeated runs; per-run peak memory. The baseline is naive PyTorch (einsum + max + sum) at matched precision (FP16 inputs, FP32 accumulation). The corpus-scaling stress test (Fig. 2) is additionally run on an A100-40GB, where the OOM cliffs fall at smaller, more accessible corpus sizes.

5.2 Forward Latency and Memory

Table 1 reports forward latency: Flash-MaxSim is faster on every shape, up to 3.9×3.9\times on A100 and 4.7×4.7\times on H100 at ColPali scale, with the gap widening as the discarded tensor grows.

HBM traffic validates the IO bound.

Table 2 reports the HBM traffic behind Theorem 1. The naive path moves 55 to 33×33\times more bytes than Flash-MaxSim (the materialized SS), saturating ≈1.3\approx\!1.3 TB/s of A100 bandwidth, i.e. it is memory-bound. Flash-MaxSim moves a constant 0.260.26 GB (inputs only) and runs near the matmul arithmetic floor (ColPali: 1.701.70 ms vs. a 1.721.72 ms floor, Table 1), confirming it has crossed from memory-bound to compute-bound.

Tile-size robustness.

Sweeping the query-chunk size (the kernel’s main tile knob) at ColPali shape, latency is flat within 3%3\% across 6464 to 512512 (1.681.68 to 1.741.74 ms) and rises to 2.862.86 ms only when chunking is disabled (Lq=1024L_{q}{=}1024 in a single block), confirming both the value of the query-chunk decomposition (§4.1) and that the kernel needs no fine per-shape tile tuning.

Memory and the OOM unlock.

Figure 2 traces corpus scaling on A100-40GB for both naive precisions; Table 3 reports peak memory at ColPali shape on A100-40GB (FP16 intermediate) and A100-80GB (matched FP32, the protocol baseline). Flash-MaxSim peak memory grows linearly, tracking the document embeddings. The naive path grows as B​Lq​LdBL_{q}L_{d} and OOMs by B=20B{=}20K on either GPU. At B=10B{=}10K Flash-MaxSim uses 8.2×8.2\times less memory than the FP16 naive path and 16×16\times less than the matched-FP32 baseline; beyond B=20B{=}20K only Flash-MaxSim runs.

5.3 Out-of-Core Corpus Scaling

Because Flash-MaxSim peak memory is set by a single streamed document block, a corpus that exceeds GPU memory can be scored by holding it in host RAM and streaming blocks to the GPU. Table 4 scores one ColPali query against corpora up to 750​K750\mathrm{K} documents (197197 GB of embeddings, 2.3×2.3\times the 8585 GB VRAM) in 20​K20\mathrm{K}-document blocks: GPU peak stays flat at ≈5.2\approx\!5.2 GB regardless of corpus size, and steady-state throughput holds at ≈52​K\approx\!52\mathrm{K} documents/s, while the naive materialized path cannot fit even B=20​KB{=}20\mathrm{K} on the GPU.

5.4 Training Step

For in-batch-negatives contrastive training at ColPali shape (Table 5), the naive backward materializes the [B,B,Lq,Ld][B,B,L_{q},L_{d}] tensor and its gradient (quadratic in BB); Flash-MaxSim’s inverse-grid CSR backward removes both. Gradients are bit-faithful: training through Flash-MaxSim reproduces the naive loss trajectory to within 0.001%0.001\% relative drift, with ∇Q/∇D\nabla Q/\nabla D cosine 1.00001.0000 against an FP32 reference.

5.5 Variable-Length Scoring

On ragged corpora, where documents are padded to a common LdmaxL_{d}^{\max} to batch them, Flash-MaxSim’s cu_seqlens variant scores only real tokens. Against the naive padded path the speedup tracks the fill ratio ρ=∑bLd(b)/(B​Ldmax)\rho=\sum_{b}L_{d}^{(b)}/(B\,L_{d}^{\max}) (Table 6): 1.61.6 to 3.0×3.0\times at a realistic (HotpotQA-like) distribution and up to 5×5\times on highly ragged corpora. The result is exact (identical scores) and compounds with the dense-forward and memory gains above.

5.6 Numerical Correctness

FP32 accumulation gives max relative error 2×10−62\times 10^{-6} vs. an FP32 reference; top-2020 ranking overlap is 100%100\% across tested shapes, confirming Proposition 1. Because the exact kernel is numerically equivalent to dense MaxSim, end-to-end retrieval quality is unchanged by construction; only the INT8×\timesINT8 path trades a controlled ranking fidelity (Spearman ρ=0.999\rho{=}0.999) for speed.

6 Conclusion

Flash-MaxSim removes the similarity tensor that bottlenecks late-interaction MaxSim, in inference and in training, exactly and in one fused pass. It is faster, uses far less memory, unlocks corpus and batch sizes PyTorch cannot reach, preserves rankings exactly, and ships open-source.

Limitations.

At very small shapes the kernel-launch overhead makes Flash-MaxSim at-parity rather than faster (the launch-bound regime). The single-step training speedup is modest at matched precision; the dominant training win is memory and the batch-size unlock, not step latency. INT8×\timesINT8 ranking is validated on text distributions; vision (ViDoRe) end-to-end nDCG parity is not yet reported and is the primary open evaluation gap.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.

Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a list of packages that need conversion, and welcome developer contributions.
